full_title: MARIZ LINDSEY TAN GANA-CARAIT Y VILLEGAS, PETITIONER, VS. COMMISSION ON ELECTIONS, ROMMEL MITRA LIM, AND DOMINIC P. NUÑEZ, RESPONDENTS.
subject: Political and Public International Law
syllabus_topic: III. Citizenship > E. Dual Citizenship and Dual Allegiance
topics: R.A. 9225 applies only to dual citizens by naturalization, not to dual citizens by birth
Material misrepresentation in the CoC (Section 78, OEC) vs. disqualification (Section 40(d), LGC)
COMELEC En Banc rulings are only executory, not final, within the 30-day Rule 64 period
Mootness exception: capable of repetition yet evading review
Foreign law is not judicially noticed and must be proved

other_subjects.subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: V. Special Civil Actions > D. Review of Commission on Elections and Commission on Audit Judgments and Final Orders or Resolutions (Rule 64)

doctrine:
**R.A. No. 9225 covers only natural-born Filipinos who became foreign citizens through naturalization.** Its twin requirements for those seeking elective office, the oath of allegiance (Section 3) and the personal and sworn renunciation of any and all foreign citizenship (Section 5(2)), **do not apply to dual citizens by birth**, whose dual citizenship results involuntarily from the concurrent application of the laws of two states. For them, the filing of the certificate of candidacy (CoC) carries an implied renunciation of foreign citizenship (Maquiling; Cordora, reiterated). Presenting documents to a foreign consulate to obtain a Consular Report of Birth Abroad stating that the person "acquired United States Citizenship at birth" only confirms citizenship acquired at birth; it is not naturalization, and positive acts done by a parent do not make the child a naturalized citizen. A dual citizen by birth who declares in her CoC that she is eligible commits no false material representation under Section 78 of the Omnibus Election Code.

Even for a naturalized dual citizen, **failure to renounce foreign citizenship under Section 5(2) of R.A. 9225 does not affect Filipino citizenship and is not an ineligibility**; it only keeps the person a dual citizen. If at all, it is a disqualification under Section 40(d) of the Local Government Code, the proper subject of a petition for disqualification, not a ground to cancel the CoC.

On procedure, the Court **harmonized** the COMELEC Rules (Rule 37, Section 3 and Rule 23, Section 8, which make decisions in CoC cases final after five days absent a restraining order) with Article IX-A, Section 7 of the Constitution and Rule 64, Section 3 (certiorari within 30 days from notice): a COMELEC En Banc ruling not restrained within five days is **only executory, not final**, so a timely Rule 64 petition may be heard despite a COMELEC certificate of finality and entry of judgment. The Court also decided the case after the term expired because the issue was capable of repetition yet evading review.
facts:
On October 17, 2018, petitioner Mariz Lindsey Tan Gana-Carait filed her CoC for Member of the Sangguniang Panlungsod of the Lone District of Biñan, Laguna for the May 13, 2019 elections. On October 22, 2018, Rommel Lim filed a petition for disqualification, alleging that she had acquired U.S. citizenship and had not made a personal and sworn renunciation of foreign citizenship. On November 6, 2018, Dominic Nuñez filed a petition to deny due course to or cancel her CoC, claiming that because she used a U.S. passport, her statements that she was a Filipino citizen and eligible were false.

Petitioner was born on June 25, 1991 in Makati City to a Filipino father and an American mother. A Consular Report of Birth Abroad (CRBA) stated that she "acquired United States Citizenship at birth as established by documentary evidence presented to the Consular Service of the United States at Manila, Philippines on August 23, 2004." She obtained a U.S. passport in 2010 and used it to travel until 2018. She had won as barangay kagawad in 2013 and as Sangguniang Panlungsod member in 2016. She answered that she was a dual citizen by birth and not covered by R.A. 9225.

In a Resolution dated February 27, 2019, the COMELEC First Division denied the disqualification petition but granted Nuñez's petition and cancelled her CoC. Relying on provisions of the U.S. Immigration and Nationality Act (cited as Acts 320 and 322), it held that she was a dual citizen by naturalization because a positive act, the presentation of documents to obtain U.S. citizenship, had been done. She therefore had to take the oath and renounce under R.A. 9225, and having failed to do so, she misrepresented her eligibility. The COMELEC En Banc denied her motion for partial reconsideration on September 23, 2021.

The COMELEC then issued a Certificate of Finality and an Entry of Judgment (both dated December 13, 2021) and a Writ of Execution (January 31, 2022). Petitioner filed a petition for certiorari under Rule 64 in relation to Rule 65 within 30 days from notice. Her term of office, which began at noon of June 30, 2019, ended at noon of June 30, 2022, before the Court decided.
issues: Whether the COMELEC En Banc Resolution had attained finality, given the COMELEC's issuance of a Certificate of Finality, Entry of Judgment and Writ of Execution.
Whether the Court should resolve the case even though petitioner's term of office had expired.
Whether petitioner is a dual citizen by birth or by naturalization, and whether the twin requirements of Sections 3 and 5(2) of R.A. 9225 apply to her.
Whether petitioner made a false material representation in her CoC that justified its cancellation.
ruling:
**1. No, the COMELEC En Banc Resolution had not become final.** Article IX-A, Section 7 of the Constitution and Rule 64, Section 3 allow an aggrieved party to bring a COMELEC ruling to the Supreme Court on certiorari within 30 days from notice. The COMELEC Rules, in contrast, count the period from promulgation (Rule 37, Section 1) and make decisions in CoC cancellation cases final and executory five days after promulgation unless restrained (Rule 37, Section 3; Rule 23, Section 8, as amended by Resolution No. 9523). Procedural rules must yield to substantive law and cannot shorten the period the Constitution grants (Treyes v. Larlar). Harmonized, COMELEC En Banc rulings not restrained by the Court within five days from receipt are **"rendered only executory — but not final."** Because the petition was timely, the resolution did not attain finality despite the Certificate of Finality and Entry of Judgment.

**2. Yes, the Court resolved the case despite mootness.** The expiration of petitioner's term at noon of June 30, 2022 (Section 43, R.A. 7160) is a supervening event that renders the case moot (Gunsi, Sr. v. COMELEC). But the question of her status, whether she is a U.S. citizen by birth or by naturalization, will come up again whenever she files a CoC. It is capable of repetition yet evading review (IBP v. Atienza), so the Court ruled on it.

**3. She is a dual citizen by birth; R.A. 9225 does not apply to her.** R.A. 9225 covers natural-born Filipinos who lost Philippine citizenship through naturalization abroad and those who, after its effectivity, become foreign citizens. Both categories refer to persons who underwent naturalization (De Guzman v. COMELEC; Tan v. Crisologo). Maquiling distinguishes dual citizens by naturalization, who must take the oath and personally renounce, from dual citizens by birth, who need not, "as the mere filing of the certificate of candidacy already carries with it an implied renunciation of foreign citizenship." The COMELEC's contrary finding was manifestly erroneous for three reasons. *First*, Philippine courts do not take judicial notice of foreign laws; the private respondents had to prove the INA provisions they relied on. *Second*, any positive act under those provisions would have been done by her American parent, and there was no evidence that she applied for U.S. citizenship or went through naturalization. *Third*, naturalization confers citizenship on an alien, so it is superfluous and absurd for one who is already a citizen. The CRBA itself states that she "acquired United States Citizenship at birth"; the documents only established that fact. As in Cordora, the process merely confirmed citizenship acquired at birth. The Court rejected the OSG's theory that R.A. 9225 covers any acquisition of foreign citizenship through a positive act, whoever performed it.

**4. No false material representation; the COMELEC gravely abused its discretion.** Since she was not covered by R.A. 9225, her non-compliance did not affect her declaration of eligibility. Even assuming she violated Section 5(2), the failure to renounce does not affect Filipino citizenship, which is retained or reacquired upon the oath of allegiance (the same oath found in the CoC). Renunciation is only a condition on the exercise of the right to seek elective office. Commonwealth Act No. 63 does not list failure to renounce as a way of losing citizenship. Remaining a dual citizen is, if at all, a disqualification under Section 40 of the LGC and the proper subject of a petition for disqualification; such a petition was filed here, dismissed, and apparently not appealed. **She therefore kept the qualification of Filipino citizenship under Section 39 of the LGC, made no false representation, and the cancellation of her CoC was grave abuse of discretion.**
disposition: The petition for certiorari was GRANTED. The COMELEC En Banc Resolution dated September 23, 2021 and the COMELEC First Division Resolution dated February 27, 2019 were ANNULLED and SET ASIDE. The Certificate of Finality and Entry of Judgment (both dated December 13, 2021) and the Writ of Execution dated January 31, 2022 were CANCELLED and SET ASIDE. Nuñez's Petition to Deny Due Course to or Cancel Certificate of Candidacy (SPA Case No. 18-126 (DC)) was DISMISSED. The Court found it unnecessary to act on the prayer for a TRO, status quo ante order or preliminary injunction.

bar_questions.q: Bianca was born in Quezon City in 1995 to a Filipino mother and a Canadian father. Assume that under Canadian law she became a Canadian citizen at birth because of her father's citizenship. In 2008, her father submitted documents to the Canadian embassy, which issued a certificate stating that Bianca "is a citizen of Canada from birth." She holds a Canadian passport. In October 2024, Bianca filed a certificate of candidacy for city councilor, declaring that she is eligible for the office. She never took an oath of allegiance under R.A. No. 9225 and never executed a sworn renunciation of her Canadian citizenship. Carlo filed a timely petition to deny due course to or cancel her CoC, alleging material misrepresentation because she did not comply with R.A. No. 9225. Will the petition prosper?

alac.answer: No. Bianca is a dual citizen by birth, so the oath and renunciation requirements of R.A. No. 9225 do not apply to her, and she made no false material representation.
alac.legal_basis: R.A. No. 9225 applies only to natural-born Filipinos who acquired foreign citizenship through naturalization. Its twin requirements, an oath of allegiance (Section 3) and a personal and sworn renunciation of foreign citizenship when the CoC is filed (Section 5(2)), bind only dual citizens by naturalization. Dual citizens by birth need not renounce, because filing a CoC carries an implied renunciation of foreign citizenship. Documents submitted to confirm foreign citizenship acquired at birth are not naturalization, especially when a parent submitted them. (Gana-Carait v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 257453, August 9, 2022, citing Maquiling v. COMELEC and Cordora v. COMELEC)
alac.application: Bianca was Filipino at birth through her mother and Canadian at birth through her father. Her dual citizenship is involuntary, the result of two states' laws applying to her at the same time. The 2008 embassy certificate, obtained by her father, only confirmed a citizenship she already had, and she never underwent naturalization. R.A. No. 9225 therefore did not require her to take the oath or renounce Canadian citizenship before running. Her declaration that she is eligible is true, so there is no false material representation under Section 78 of the Omnibus Election Code.
alac.conclusion: Carlo's petition should be dismissed because Bianca, a dual citizen by birth, made no false material representation in her CoC.

bar_questions.q: Dante, a natural-born Filipino, moved to the United States and, as an adult, applied for and was granted U.S. citizenship by naturalization in 2012. In 2023 he took the oath of allegiance under R.A. No. 9225 before a Philippine consulate. In October 2024 he filed a CoC for municipal mayor, declaring that he is a Filipino citizen eligible for the office, but he never executed a personal and sworn renunciation of his U.S. citizenship. (a) Was Dante required to renounce his U.S. citizenship? (b) His rival filed a petition under Section 78 of the Omnibus Election Code to cancel Dante's CoC, arguing that the failure to renounce made his declaration of eligibility false. Is a Section 78 petition the proper remedy?

alac.answer: (a) Yes. As a dual citizen by naturalization, Dante had to take the oath of allegiance and also make a personal and sworn renunciation of his U.S. citizenship. (b) No. His failure to renounce does not make him ineligible. At most it is a ground for disqualification under Section 40(d) of the Local Government Code, which must be raised in a petition for disqualification.
alac.legal_basis: Under Sections 3 and 5(2) of R.A. No. 9225, dual citizens by naturalization must take the oath of allegiance and personally renounce foreign citizenship when they file their CoC in order to qualify for elective office (Maquiling v. COMELEC). In Gana-Carait v. COMELEC (G.R. No. 257453, August 9, 2022), the Court held that failure to renounce under Section 5(2) does not affect the person's Filipino citizenship, which is retained or reacquired upon the oath of allegiance; it only keeps him a dual citizen. Such failure is not an ineligibility. If at all, it is a disqualification under Section 40 of the LGC and the proper subject of a petition for disqualification.
alac.application: Dante acquired U.S. citizenship through his own application for naturalization, so R.A. No. 9225 covers him, and he had to make a personal and sworn renunciation when he filed his CoC. But because he took the oath of allegiance in 2023, he is a Filipino citizen and has that qualification under Section 39 of the LGC, so his statement that he is a Filipino citizen is true. His failure to renounce leaves him a dual citizen, which bears on disqualification under Section 40(d) of the LGC, not on eligibility. A Section 78 petition, which rests on a false material representation about eligibility, is the wrong remedy; his rival should file a petition for disqualification.
alac.conclusion: Dante had to renounce his U.S. citizenship, but his failure to do so is a matter for a petition for disqualification, not a ground to cancel his CoC under Section 78.

bar_questions.q: The COMELEC En Banc affirmed the cancellation of Ellen's certificate of candidacy for city councilor on the ground that she was a foreign citizen by naturalization who had not complied with R.A. No. 9225. Ellen filed a petition for certiorari under Rule 64 with the Supreme Court within the reglementary period from her receipt of the En Banc resolution. Since no restraining order was issued within five days, the COMELEC issued a certificate of finality, an entry of judgment and a writ of execution. By the time the Court took up the case, the term for which Ellen ran had expired. The COMELEC argues that (a) its resolution has become final and can no longer be reviewed, and (b) the case is moot. Rule on both arguments.

alac.answer: (a) The argument fails. The resolution was only executory, not final, so the Court may still review it. (b) The case is moot, but the Court may still decide it because the issue is capable of repetition yet evading review.
alac.legal_basis: Article IX-A, Section 7 of the Constitution and Rule 64, Section 3 of the Rules of Court give an aggrieved party 30 days from notice to bring a COMELEC ruling to the Supreme Court on certiorari. The COMELEC Rules that make En Banc rulings final five days after promulgation or receipt absent a restraining order (Rule 37, Section 3; Rule 23, Section 8, as amended by Resolution No. 9523) are procedural. They must be harmonized with the Constitution: within the 30-day period, such rulings are executory but not final. The expiration of the term makes a CoC case moot, but the Court may decide it when the issue is capable of repetition yet evading review. (Gana-Carait v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 257453, August 9, 2022)
alac.application: Ellen filed within the period, so the COMELEC's certificate of finality, entry of judgment and writ of execution did not make the resolution final. At most the resolution could be executed. The Court may review it and, if it finds grave abuse of discretion, set aside even the certificate of finality and the writ of execution. On mootness, the expiration of the term is a supervening event, but the question of Ellen's citizenship status will come up again every time she files a CoC, and the short terms involved make it likely to evade review again. This falls within the exception.
alac.conclusion: The Court may take cognizance of Ellen's petition despite the COMELEC's certificate of finality and the expiration of the term.

notes: Leonen, SAJ., Caguioa, J., and Lazaro-Javier, J. wrote separate concurring opinions, which are not examinable. The main opinion adopts some of their points (credited in its footnotes), and those points are part of the ponencia. Inting and Kho, Jr., JJ. took no part; M. Lopez, J. was on official leave. The decision cites the constitutional provision as "Section 7, Article IX"; it is the common provision on the Constitutional Commissions (Article IX-A).
